newsitem.title: USA: EMU entrants must meet Maastricht terms - Finland.
newsitem.headline: EMU entrants must meet Maastricht terms - Finland.

text.p: Membership of European monetary union in 1999 must be based purely on whether a country fulfils criteria in the Maastricht treaty, Finnish Finance Minister Sauli Niinisto said on Tuesday.

He had been asked whether European Union member states would look at other factors, including medium-term sustainability of budget deficit reduction programmes, in deciding who would join a single currency in 1999.

"I think there is no possibility to think that way. The question is quite simply, if you fulfil all the criteria you are in," he told Reuters in an interview at the annual meeting of the International Monetary Fund and World Bank.

He declined to make any specific comment on whether Italy, which has made a huge effort to reduce its budget deficit with a special EU tax, would make it into monetary union, saying the question of who joined first was up to the EU to decide at the appropriate time.
"We are not speculating if there will be more or less countries," he said.
EU leaders will decide by June 1998 which countries join a single currency first, based on fiscal and monetary performances in 1997. Finland is expected to meet the criteria.

Niinisto said it would be "very peculiar" if countries were excluded from the first wave of monetary union if their currencies had not been a member of the European Exchange Rate Mechanism (ERM) in the two years prior to the decision -- rather than the two years prior to the single currency launch.
"That would be a very peculiar situation. Everybody knows there is time from spring 1998 to January 1, 1999," he said.
Any insistence on ERM membership for two years prior to the decision on who joins -- as opposed to two years prior to the launch in January 1999 -- would exclude Finland and Italy.

Both are considering bringing their currencies into the Exchange Rate Mechanism, though Niinisto declined to say when the markka might join the ERM, beyond repeating that Finland planned to take a decision in the autumn.

Niinisto said however that EU plans to set up an ERM II after monetary union -- for currencies whose countries are waiting to join -- made it seem more necessary that those who wanted to join first should be a member of ERM I.

The Maastricht treaty is ambiguous on a requirement that countries should have shown currency stability for two years in order to qualify for monetary union, making no specific reference to the ERM. Ministers have yet to decide how they will interpret its provisions on currency stabilty.
"In the springtime it became more and more obvious that joining the ERM might be necessary on the basis of the criteria," he said.
If EU leaders decided in early 1998 that it was not necessary to have been a member of ERM I to qualify, "what would that mean for the new ERM II?"
"There is a strong will to form a new ERM. With the fact that there is an ERM II coming, it is more obvious you have to be a member of ERM I," he said.
